doc.title: Vincent Pelote interviewed by Monk Rowe, Orlando, Florida, February 25, 2017

chapter: Becoming a jazz fan and musician
title: Growing up in Jersey City: uncle, father's records and guitar
summary: Pelote's uncle Lester was a jazz guitarist, his father played Wes Montgomery and Al Casey records, and he began on guitar; he also remembers 'Hello Dolly'.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: So I saw a video of you, I guess it was taken at the Association of Recorded Sound Collections.
And you were saying different people collect different things, and we all have our passions.
So what was your passion as a young man.

My passion as a young man was always, like most kids I listened to the popular music of the day, I had my little transistor radio. Remember those little 9-volt transistor radios you used to put to your ear? Or you had the one earphone that stuck in. Yeah. So I had that and I generally listened to the black stations on the other end of the dial, you know, WWRL and I liked Motown and all that. But then my uncle, Lester Pelote, was a professional jazz guitarist in New York. He never really broke out of the local scene and eventually became a cab driver and that was pretty much it. But he used to come to the house a lot, in Jersey City, and visit his brother, my father. And I got interested in guitar at that point. And my father, who wasn’t a musician but who liked jazz and had really two jazz albums that he played consistently, especially when he was a little drunk, he played the Wes Montgomery Trio on the Riverside label, the first album that Wes ever made, and an album that Al Casey, they called “Buck Jumpin’ on Swingville Prestige. And he played those two records over and over and over again to the point where my sisters were complaining about it — stop it, dad. But you know I saw him listening to them and to me, as a budding guitarist, because I was interested in playing guitar because of my uncle so I was fussing around with it, I was listening to this and I said yea, I like Wes. Al Casey is more approachable. I can copy him better. Because it was mostly single note stuff and it was a simpler style, a simpler single string style, because he goes back to the 30s, and Wes was more of a post-bop guitarist, even though he started out playing Charlie Christian solos. And so his stuff was hard. And then the octave thing which was completely out of my — I didn’t know what the hell was even going on with that. And of course soloing in chords, using block chords was completely like — you know. So I fell in love with the Al Casey album first. But then I started listening to more and more Wes and he became my hero. And so my passion became that, and also again, I have to point to my sister’s collection. She had the record “Hello Dolly” in her 45 collection. Now I know it was a big hit in ’64, it knocked The Beatles off the chart that year, but I didn’t really dig the record until 1966, ’67, ’66. And I started playing it and listening to it and I liked it. I liked the other side better by the way, “A Lot of Living to do” was the other side of that record, the 45.
